title: 2 Kings 15:1–7
context: Azariah, also called Uzziah in this chapter (15:13, 32) and in Chronicles, begins a fifty-two-year reign in Judah. He does what is right, as his father Amaziah did, yet the high places remain. The LORD strikes him with leprosy, and he lives in a separate house while his son Jotham governs. Second Chronicles 26 gives the fuller account, explaining that his heart was lifted up and he entered the temple to burn incense.

verses.text: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah begins to reign in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam II of Israel. Arminian readers note that Kings dates each king by the other kingdom, keeping both halves of God's divided people in view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the synchronized dating reminds readers that both kingdoms remain under one Lord. Judah and Israel are judged by the same covenant standard, whatever their separate histories.

verses.text: He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: He becomes king at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years; his mother is Jecoliah. Arminian readers note the long reign as an extended opportunity, given by God, to lead Judah in faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a reign of fifty-two years is a remarkable gift of stability. Second Chronicles 26:5 adds that "as long as he sought the LORD, God made him prosper."

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.
verses.arminianNotes: He does what is right "according to all that his father Amaziah had done." Arminian readers note that the verdict is positive but measured, matching a father whose faithfulness was also incomplete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the comparison is to Amaziah, not David. The verdict is genuine but qualified, which prepares readers for the limits named in the next verses.

verses.text: However, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
verses.arminianNotes: "However, the high places were not taken away." Arminian readers see that a king's personal faithfulness did not extend to reforming the nation's worship, a failure of leadership that left the people in compromise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this refrain recurs through the good kings of Judah until Hezekiah. Partial reform leaves deep-rooted patterns of false worship in place among God's people.

verses.text: The LORD struck the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and lived in a separate house. Jotham, the king’s son, was over the household, judging the people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD struck the king" with leprosy, and he lives apart while Jotham rules. Arminian readers note that 2 Chronicles 26:16 explains why: "his heart was lifted up" and he went in to burn incense, a choice that brought discipline.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Kings simply credits the LORD with the affliction, while Chronicles supplies the cause. Even a long and blessed reign remains under God's hand, and pride is not overlooked.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Azariah's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note how briefly Kings treats so long a reign, focusing on his worship and discipline rather than achievements.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator's selectivity shows his purpose. Fifty-two years are summarized in a few lines because the writer's concern is covenant faithfulness, not political history.

verses.text: Azariah slept with his fathers; and they buried him with his fathers in David’s city; and Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Azariah is buried with his fathers in David's city, and Jotham succeeds him. Arminian readers note that, though disciplined, he receives a king's burial, showing that God's discipline did not erase his place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah 6:1 dates the prophet's vision to "the year that King Uzziah died." As an earthly king's long reign ends, Isaiah sees the Lord "sitting on a throne, high and lifted up."
